landing.free: Every lesson is free to read. Sign up to keep your progress, quiz results and review cards.
landing.resourcesBody: The textbooks, lectures, papers, code and datasets chosen for each lesson, in one place.
landing.h1: Learn robotics, from the basics to research level
landing.lead: Free robotics tutorials that lay out what to study and in what order — for someone learning robotics for the first time and for someone preparing for graduate-level research. Every lesson comes with a study plan, recommended resources and a quiz, in English and Korean.
landing.whatTitle: What you learn in these robotics tutorials
landing.whatBody: Everything needed to make a robot move, perceive its surroundings and decide for itself, in order. These are the modules of the Robotics Expert Course.
landing.how1Body: Modules and lessons show a recommended order and their prerequisites, so you always know what to study next.
landing.how2Title: A study plan for every lesson
landing.how2Body: Each lesson says what to read first, what to derive yourself and how to check your understanding, with recommended textbooks, lecture videos and papers.
landing.how3Body: A quiz at the end of each lesson checks your understanding; the questions you miss and the key concepts become spaced-repetition review cards.
landing.how4Body: Sign up to record study time and completed lessons, and look back on your week in a weekly report.
landing.faq1Q: I am new to robotics. Where do I start?
landing.faq1A: Start with the first module of the Robotics Expert Course (maths and physics foundations) and follow the roadmap in order. Prerequisites are advice, not locks, so you can skip a module you already know.
landing.faq2A: Yes. Every lesson and the resource library are free to read. An account is only needed to save your progress, quiz results and review cards.
landing.faq3Q: What do I need to know before I start?
landing.faq3A: High-school mathematics is enough to begin. The maths you need — vectors, matrices, coordinate transforms — is covered in the first module. The example code is in Python, so being able to read Python helps.
landing.faq4Q: How long does it take to finish?
landing.faq4A: The Robotics Expert Course has {expertLessons} lessons and takes about {expertHours} hours of study. The researcher track has {researchLessons} lessons and takes far longer, because it includes paper reading and reproduction tasks.
landing.faq5Q: Do I need a robot or a simulator?
landing.faq5A: No. The lessons, quizzes and the calculation and implementation problems can all be done on a laptop. This site does not integrate a simulator; public tools and datasets you can practise with are linked in the resource library.
landing.faq6Q: Is it available in Korean as well?
landing.faq6A: Yes. Every lesson is available in English and Korean. Switch with the language selector at the top of the page.

guide.title: How to learn robotics
guide.lead: Robotics ties together mathematics, control, perception and software, which makes it hard to decide what to study first. This guide lays out an order and a method that someone learning on their own can follow, based on the robotics tutorials on this site.
guide.beforeBody: High-school mathematics and the ability to read Python are enough. The maths robotics needs, such as linear algebra and coordinate transforms, is covered in the first module, so you can begin without a separate preparation phase. You do not need a robot or a simulator.
guide.pathTitle: What to learn, and in what order
guide.pathBody: These are the stages of the {course}. Each stage is the prerequisite of the next, and the time shown is the sum of the estimated study time of its lessons.
guide.stageSummary: {modules, plural, one {# module} other {# modules}} · {lessons} lessons · about {hours} hours
guide.lessonTitle: How to work through one lesson
guide.lessonBody: A lesson is a procedure to follow, not an article to read once. Every lesson has the same structure.
guide.step1Body: “How to study this stage” at the top of the lesson says what to look at, in what order and for how long.
guide.step2Body: Derive the key formulas yourself instead of only reading them, and work the examples through with numbers.
guide.step3Title: Fill gaps with the recommended resources
guide.step3Body: Where you get stuck, read the linked textbook chapter or watch the linked lecture.
guide.step4Body: Take the quiz at the end of the lesson. The questions you miss become review cards, with their explanations.
guide.step5Title: Come back to the review cards
guide.step5Body: Working through the cards as the spaced-repetition schedule brings them back is what makes the material stay.
guide.researchBody: After the foundations you can continue with the {course}. It works at the level of graduate courses and papers from the international conferences: in every lesson you derive the key results, read the original papers and reproduce them numerically.
guide.tip1: Study in short, frequent sessions rather than long, rare ones. If you log your study time, the weekly report shows the pattern.
guide.tip2: Skip a module you already know. Prerequisites are advice, not locks.
guide.tip3: Move on when you can do the quiz and the problems, not when the text merely feels familiar.
guide.startBody: Open the first lesson from the roadmap.
